spec.section: The Language / Expressions / Raising to a power
spec.requirement: The right side of 'ⁿ' is an integer.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEOF_TAKES_A_LIFT
diagnostics.message: '⎕typeof' takes something lifted, written between '⌜' and '⌝'
diagnostics.cause: A type's name and a value's name are both identifiers, and a type written out in full is not an expression at all, so what follows `⎕typeof` cannot be read without knowing what the names turned out to mean.  The brackets say it instead: `⎕typeof(⌜a⌝)` asks about the name `a`, whatever `a` is, and the grammar never has to guess.

spec.section: The Language / Settled while compiling / Lifting
spec.requirement: The argument of '⎕typeof' is a lift.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEOF_OF_A_TYPE
diagnostics.message: '⎕typeof' asks what something is of, and '{found}' is already a type
diagnostics.cause: A type lifted out of the program is already the answer this would give, so asking it of one is asking a question with nothing behind it.  There is no type of a type here: a type is not a value, which is what lets the whole of this be settled while compiling and nothing of it reach the program.

spec.section: The Language / Settled while compiling / Lifting
spec.requirement: '⎕typeof' is asked of a lifted expression.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LIFT_IS_NOT_A_VALUE
diagnostics.message: what is lifted out of the program is not a value, and this is where a value stands
diagnostics.cause: Lifting something takes it out of the program and hands it to the compiler, which has no representation to give back: a type is not a value here and neither is a name.  The places a lift may stand are the ones where the compiler answers rather than the program computes -- inside `⎕typeof`, on either side of a comparison the compiler settles, and after `⌈` or `⌊`, where what it answers is the largest or smallest value the lifted type has.

spec.section: The Language / Settled while compiling / Lifting
spec.requirement: A lift stands where the compiler answers and nowhere else.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMERATE_IS_NOT_A_VALUE
diagnostics.message: '⎕enumerate' makes something for a loop to walk, and this is not where a loop takes its values from
diagnostics.cause: What it makes is an iterator, and a loop is the only thing that takes one: there is no type for an iterator in this language and nothing else to do with one.  So it stands after the `=` of a `foreach` and nowhere else.

spec.requirement: '⎕enumerate' stands where a loop takes its values from.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMERATE_TAKES_ONE_OR_TWO
diagnostics.message: '⎕enumerate' takes what to walk, and optionally what to count from; {found} were written
diagnostics.cause: One argument is the thing to walk, counting from zero.  A second says what to count from instead, and its type is the type the count has -- so `⎕enumerate(v, 1u8)` counts in bytes from one.  There is no third thing to say: how far the count moves each turn is one, which is what counting is.

spec.requirement: '⎕enumerate' takes one argument or two.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMERATE_COUNTS_IN_INTEGERS
diagnostics.message: '⎕enumerate' counts the turns, and '{found}' is not a number to count in

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what it was told to count from

diagnostics.cause: What it counts from says what type the count has, and a count is a whole number.  The count goes up by one each turn and is checked like every other addition, so a count that runs past the end of its type stops the program -- which is what says the type was too narrow for the thing being walked.

spec.requirement: The second argument of '⎕enumerate' is an integer.

diagnostics.name: LANG_DIVIDES_IS_FOR_INTEGERS
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' asks whether one number divides another with nothing left over, and '{found}' is not a whole number

args.name: operator
args.description: which of the two was written

diagnostics.cause: Dividing without a remainder is a question about whole numbers: what is left over is what the question is about, and a floating-point division leaves nothing over by construction. spec.section: The Language / Expressions / Dividing without a remainder
spec.requirement: The operands of '∣' are integers.

diagnostics.name: LANG_DIVIDES_NEEDS_A_TWO
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' written before one operand asks whether two divides it, and '{found}' has no two

args.name: operator
args.description: which of the two was written

diagnostics.cause: Written before one operand it is the same operator with two on the left, so it needs a two of the operand's own type -- and a type of one bit has not got one.  What was meant is a question about that one bit, and comparing it with nothing or with one says it.

spec.section: The Language / Expressions / Dividing without a remainder
spec.requirement: '∣' written before one operand needs a type that holds two.

diagnostics.name: LANG_DIVIDES_BY_A_WRITTEN_ZERO
diagnostics.message: nothing divides by zero, and '{operator}' written with a zero on the left asks whether it does

args.name: operator
args.description: which of the two was written

diagnostics.cause: Where the divisor is written down the operator answers a truth value, there being no pair of operands it has no answer for -- except this one.  A divisor the program works out may turn out to be zero and the answer is a result, which has somewhere to say so; a zero written down has nowhere, and a program that wrote one asked a question it knew the answer to.

spec.section: The Language / Expressions / Dividing without a remainder
spec.requirement: A zero written on the left of '∣' is refused.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_BOTTOM_CARRIES_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: the error of '{found}' carries nothing, so there is nothing for a name here to stand for
diagnostics.cause: A result whose type names what its error carries -- `bool?u8` -- has something for the arm written `⊥` to bind; one written `bool?` has not, its error being the fact that there is no answer and nothing more.  A name written there would stand for nothing, which is a thing to say rather than a thing to allow.

spec.requirement: A name in a '⊥' arm needs an error that carries something.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FAILURE_NEEDS_A_RESULT
diagnostics.message: '⊥' is a result that has no answer, and this is where {found} stands

args.name: found
args.description: what was wanted where it was written

diagnostics.cause: What it is a failure *of* is not written with it: it is whatever stands where it stands, exactly as a value of the answer type written there is the successful result of the same type.  So it needs somewhere that wants a result -- the answer of a function that answers one, a variable whose type says one, an argument of a parameter that takes one -- and somewhere that wants anything else has nothing for it to be.

spec.requirement: '⊥' stands where a result is wanted.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FAILURE_CARRIES_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: the error of '{found}' carries nothing, so there is nothing for this value to be
diagnostics.cause: A result written `TYPE?` has an error that is the fact that there is no answer and nothing more; one written `TYPE?ERROR` has an error that carries a value.  Which of the two is being made is the type it is being made as, and a value written for an error that has nowhere to put it is a value nothing would ever read.

spec.requirement: '⊥' carries a value only where the error does.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FAILURE_NEEDS_A_VALUE
diagnostics.message: the error of '{found}' carries a {carried}, and none is written here
diagnostics.cause: A result whose type says its error carries a value has one in every failure of it: there is no failure of such a type that carries nothing, so a `⊥` written without a value would be making a value with a hole in it.  What to write there is whatever the error is to say.

spec.requirement: '⊥' carries a value where the error does.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PARAM_DEFAULT_NOT_SETTLED
diagnostics.message: what '{name}' is given where a caller says nothing has to be settled while compiling
diagnostics.cause: A default belongs to every call of the function, including calls in other files, and a caller there cannot see the names the definition could.  So what is written has to be a value the compiler settles where the function is defined, and is then the same value at every call.  That is a narrower rule than C++'s, which looks the names up at the definition and computes them at the call; it is what this language can promise without a scope travelling with the function.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: A parameter's default is settled while compiling.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PARAM_DEFAULT_ORDER
diagnostics.message: '{name}' has no default and follows one that has, so a call that leaves it out would have nothing to leave out
diagnostics.cause: Arguments written without a name fill the parameters from the left, so a parameter with a default before one without means a call giving one argument fewer cannot say which it left out.  Every parameter after one with a default therefore has one too.  Naming the arguments is what gets round it -- but the rule is about what a call *without* names can mean.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Every parameter after one with a default has one.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_UNKNOWN_PARAMETER
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not a parameter of '{func}'
diagnostics.cause: An argument that names its parameter names one the function has.  A name that is not one of them is usually a spelling, and the parameters are where to look for the right one.

spec.requirement: A named argument names a parameter of the function.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_PARAMETER_TWICE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is given twice
diagnostics.cause: A parameter takes one argument.  It is given twice where a name repeats one an earlier argument already filled -- by its place or by its own name -- and which of the two was meant is not something to guess at.

spec.requirement: A parameter is given one argument.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_POSITION_AFTER_NAME
diagnostics.message: this argument does not name its parameter, and one before it did
diagnostics.cause: An argument that does not name its parameter is for the parameter in the place it stands, and once an argument has named one the places no longer say which is which.  So the ones written by place come first and the ones written by name come after, which is the order they read in anyway.

spec.requirement: An argument written by place comes before every argument written by name.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_PARAMETER_MISSING
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is given nothing and has no default
diagnostics.cause: Every parameter has a value at every call: one the call wrote, by place or by name, or the default the definition wrote.  A parameter with neither is a call the function cannot be entered with.

spec.requirement: Every parameter is given a value or has a default.

diagnostics.name: LANG_REF_ANSWERED
diagnostics.message: a function may not answer with something that holds a reference
diagnostics.cause: A function answering with a reference says how long what it names lives -- `static` in the type, or `from` naming the parameter it was borrowed from.  Neither can be written about a reference inside something else: `static` belongs to the reference and there may be several, and `from` speaks for the whole answer.  So a tuple, a product or a collection holding one may not be answered with, and the reference is handed back on its own instead.

spec.requirement: A reference does not leave the call that made it.

diagnostics.name: LANG_REF_AT_TOP_LEVEL
diagnostics.message: a variable at the top level holds a reference only where it says 'static'
diagnostics.cause: A variable at the top level lasts as long as the program, so what it names has to as well.  That is exactly what `static` in the type promises, and nothing else does: a reference borrowed from a parameter lives only as long as the call that made it, and one put here by that call would outlive what it pointed at.  It is the same question a function answering with a reference is asked, at the other place a value can escape to.

spec.requirement: A reference does not leave the call that made it.

diagnostics.name: LANG_REF_NOT_A_PLACE
diagnostics.message: '&' needs a place, and this is a value
diagnostics.cause: A reference names somewhere, so what follows `&` has to be something that is somewhere: a name, a variable at the top level, an element of an array.  A value the program worked out is in no particular place -- it may be in a register and it may be nowhere at all -- so there is nothing for a reference to name.

spec.requirement: '&' is written before a place.

diagnostics.name: LANG_DEREF_NOT_A_REFERENCE
diagnostics.message: '⌖' reads through a reference, and '{found}' is not one

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was written

diagnostics.cause: The mark after a value says to read what is at the place it names, which only a reference names.  Written after anything else there is no place to read.

spec.requirement: '⌖' is written after a reference.

diagnostics.name: LANG_REF_NOT_WRITABLE
diagnostics.message: '{found}' does not allow what it names to be written
diagnostics.cause: Whether the place may be written is part of a reference's type, because the one who wrote the reference and the one who reads it both reach that place: `&mut T` allows it and `&T` does not.  That is where it differs from the `mut` a variable carries, which says only that the name may be bound to something else.

spec.requirement: Writing through a reference needs '&mut'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_REF_TYPE_NOT_ALLOWED
diagnostics.message: a reference may not name a place holding '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: One value in one place is what a reference names.  An array, a list, a string, a set, a dictionary, a tuple and a result are each already several values or already a place, so a reference to one would be a second way of writing what a value of it is.

spec.requirement: A reference names a place holding one value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_UNIT_UNKNOWN
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not a unit
diagnostics.cause: The units the language provides are the SI base units and the two the compiler counts with.  Any other is introduced by a `unit` definition before it is used, which is what keeps a unit mistyped in one place from quietly becoming a unit of its own -- the mistake a language with no such rule cannot tell from a new kind of quantity.

spec.requirement: A unit is builtin or introduced with 'unit'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_UNIT_NOT_A_NUMBER
diagnostics.message: a unit belongs to a number, and '{found}' is not one
diagnostics.cause: A unit says what a number counts.  A truth value counts nothing, a code point counts nothing, and an array is several of something whose unit belongs to what it holds -- which is where it is written, `u8 ¤meter⟦4⟧` being four lengths.

spec.requirement: A unit is written after a number type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_UNIT_INDEX
diagnostics.message: an index counts places, so it needs '¤idx', and this is '{found}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was written

diagnostics.cause: Which element of an array is wanted is not a length, a count of seconds or a number of apples, and an index worked out from one of those is nearly always a mistake.  The unit of the question -- which one -- is `¤idx`, and a number with another unit reaches it through `⎕drop` and `⎕unit`, which is the program saying it meant to.

spec.requirement: An index has the unit '¤idx'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_UNIT_ALREADY_DEFINED
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is already a unit here
diagnostics.cause: A unit is introduced once where it is introduced at all.  Two definitions of one name would be two units a reader could not tell apart, or one definition saying two things about the same unit.

spec.requirement: A unit is introduced once.

diagnostics.name: LANG_UNIT_DROP_HAS_NONE
diagnostics.message: '⎕drop' takes a unit off, and this value has none
diagnostics.cause: What it does is cross from a type with a unit to the one without it, and a value that has no unit is already there.  A call that does nothing is a line a generator emitted by mistake, which is what every rule about a statement with no effect is for.

spec.requirement: '⎕drop' is written where there is a unit.

diagnostics.name: LANG_UNIT_PUT_ON_A_UNIT
diagnostics.message: '⎕unit' puts a unit on a number that has none, and this one has '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: Nothing crosses from one unit to another in a single step, because a step that did would be the mistake units exist to catch written in one place instead of none.  A value that has a unit reaches another through `⎕drop` and then `⎕unit`, which is two things said out loud.

spec.requirement: '⎕unit' is written where there is no unit.

diagnostics.name: LANG_UNIT_TAKES_TWO
diagnostics.message: '{name}' takes {wanted} arguments, and {found} were written
diagnostics.cause: `⎕drop` takes the value whose unit is to come off; `⎕unit` and `⎕narrow` take that value and, between the lifting marks, the unit or the type -- which are lifted because both are something the compiler reads and neither is a value the program works out.

spec.requirement: '⎕drop' takes one argument and '⎕unit' two.

diagnostics.name: LANG_UNIT_NOT_LIFTED
diagnostics.message: the unit '⎕unit' puts on is written between '⌜' and '⌝'
diagnostics.cause: A unit is not a value: there is nothing at all for one to be at the time the program runs, since a unit is the part of a type the code knows nothing about.  So it is lifted out of the program the same way a type is where the compiler is asked about one.

spec.requirement: The unit is written between the lifting marks.

diagnostics.name: LANG_NARROW_NOT_A_TYPE
diagnostics.message: the type '⎕narrow' makes a value of is written between '⌜' and '⌝'
diagnostics.cause: A type is not a value, so it is lifted out of the program the way it is everywhere the compiler is asked about one.  Without the marks the name would be read as a value's, a type's name and a value's name being both identifiers, and which was meant would depend on what the name turned out to be.

spec.requirement: The type is written between the lifting marks.

diagnostics.name: LANG_NARROW_NOT_AN_INTEGER
diagnostics.message: '⎕narrow' makes a whole number out of a whole number, and '{found}' is not one
diagnostics.cause: Whether a value fits is a question about the ends of a type, and the types that have ends a value can fall outside are the whole numbers.  A floating-point number narrowed to a whole one is a different question -- it asks what to do with what is after the point -- and nothing in the language answers it yet.

spec.requirement: '⎕narrow' is written of a whole number and to one.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LAMBDA_ANSWERED
diagnostics.message: a function may not answer with something that holds a lambda
diagnostics.cause: A lambda keeps what it brought in, and what it brought in lives in the call that wrote it -- so handing one back would hand back a way of reading storage that is gone.  It is the rule a reference follows, at the same place and for the same reason, and lifetime annotations are what will lift both.

spec.requirement: A lambda does not leave the call that made it.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LAMBDA_AT_TOP_LEVEL
diagnostics.message: a variable at the top level may not hold a lambda
diagnostics.cause: A variable here lasts as long as the program, so what a lambda kept would have to as well -- and what it kept belongs to the call that wrote it.  It is the rule about answering with one, asked at the other place a value can escape to.

spec.requirement: A lambda does not leave the call that made it.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CAPTURE_UNKNOWN
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is brought in and is not a name here

args.name: name
args.description: the name in the capture list

diagnostics.cause: A capture list names what the body may reach from around it, so every name in it is one the place the lambda is written can see.  A name that is not is a spelling, or a name that belongs somewhere else.

spec.requirement: A capture names something bound where the lambda is written.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CAPTURE_NOT_LISTED
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not a parameter and was not brought in
diagnostics.cause: A lambda reads its parameters, what it brought in, and what the whole program has -- and nothing else.  A name from around it that is not in the capture list is one the body may not reach, which is the whole point of the list: what a lambda depends on is written at the top of it rather than found by reading the body.

spec.requirement: A lambda reads its parameters, its captures and the top level.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CAPTURE_TWICE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is brought in twice
diagnostics.cause: A name is brought in once, by value or by reference.  Twice would be two ways of reaching one variable inside one body, and which of them a mention meant would not be decidable.

spec.requirement: A name is brought in once.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CAPTURE_NOT_USED
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is brought in and the body does not use it
diagnostics.cause: A capture list says what a lambda depends on, so a name in it that the body never reaches is a thing the list says and the lambda does not do.  It costs room in what the lambda carries and a copy where it is written, and -- worse than either -- it tells a reader the lambda depends on something it does not.  A list that says `=` or `&` brings in what the body reaches and cannot bring in too much, so one that does is the compiler having got it wrong rather than the program.

spec.requirement: Everything a capture list brings in is used.

diagnostics.name: LANG_GENERIC_NOT_DETERMINED
diagnostics.message: nothing at a call could say what '{name}' is
diagnostics.cause: The types a generic function is called with are worked out from the types of its arguments, so a type parameter that stands nowhere among them is one no call could settle.  Written only in what the function answers with, it would have to be said at the call -- and there is no way to say it, on purpose: a call that wrote its types would be a second way of saying what the arguments already say everywhere else.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Generic Functions
spec.requirement: Every type parameter stands in a parameter's type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_GENERIC_NOT_MATCHED
diagnostics.message: what '{name}' is cannot be worked out from this argument
diagnostics.cause: The type a parameter is written with says how to read the argument's type: `T’⟦⟧` against `u8⟦4⟧` says `T’` is `u8`.  Where the two are not the same shape there is nothing to read, and what the type parameter is stays unknown.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Generic Functions
spec.requirement: An argument's type has the shape the parameter was written with.

diagnostics.name: LANG_GENERIC_TWO_WAYS
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is '{first}' from one argument and '{second}' from another
diagnostics.cause: A type parameter is one type in one call, so two arguments that say different things about it are two arguments that cannot both be right.  Nothing is widened to make them meet, here as everywhere else.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Generic Functions
spec.requirement: A type parameter is one type in one call.

diagnostics.name: LANG_GENERIC_IS_SPECIAL
diagnostics.message: '{name}' has type parameters and '{attribute}', which cannot both be true
diagnostics.cause: A function with type parameters is written once and compiled once for each set of types a call gives it, so there is no one function for something outside to reach: the runtime's entry point, a constructor and a test are each one thing the program has, and a template is none.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Generic Functions
spec.requirement: A function the runtime or another image reaches has no type parameters.

diagnostics.name: LANG_GENERIC_ASKED_HERE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' was compiled for {types} because of this call

args.name: types
args.description: the types it was compiled for

diagnostics.cause: The body of a generic function is checked for each set of types a call gives it, so what is wrong with it is wrong for those types and not for the function.  The message points at the line the mistake is written on, which is in the definition; this says which call asked for it, which is the thing a reader cannot see from there.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Generic Functions
spec.requirement: A generic function's body is checked for each set of types.

diagnostics.name: LANG_REF_PLACE_NOT_MUTABLE
diagnostics.message: '&mut' needs a place that may be changed, and '{name}' may not be
diagnostics.cause: A reference that allows writing is a way to write the place, so the place has to be one the program could have written where it stands.  A name defined without `mut` is not, and neither is a variable at the top level defined without it.

spec.requirement: '&mut' is written before a place that may be changed.

diagnostics.name: LANG_BORROW_NOT_FROM_IT
diagnostics.message: what this answers with does not name anything '{name}' named
diagnostics.cause: `from` is a promise to the caller: the answer lives as long as what that parameter named, so the caller may keep it that long.  A reference made out of this call's own storage does not, and a reference made out of another parameter lives as long as *that* one -- which is a different promise and may be a shorter one.

spec.requirement: What a function answers with comes from the parameter it says it does.

diagnostics.name: LANG_BORROW_SAYS_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: a function answering with a reference says how long it lives: 'static' or a lifetime name
diagnostics.cause: A reference is only worth having while what it names is still there, and a caller cannot see into the function to work that out.  So a function that hands one back says which of the two it is: as long as the program, which `static` in the type says, or as long as whatever else in the signature carries the same lifetime name, which `⧖x` says.  Without either there is nothing a caller could safely do with it.

spec.requirement: A function answering with a reference says how long it lives.

diagnostics.name: LANG_BORROW_ALIASED

spec.requirement: A '&mut' is the only reference to its place while it lives; a '&' may share with other '&'s.

diagnostics.name: LANG_BORROW_LENT_HERE

args.name: name
args.description: the name the reference was taken of

diagnostics.cause: Points at the reference that is still alive, which is the thing a reader cannot see from where the second one is written.

spec.requirement: A '&mut' is the only reference to its place while it lives; a '&' may share with other '&'s.

diagnostics.name: LANG_BORROW_NAME_READ

args.description: the name that was lent out

spec.requirement: A '&mut' is the only reference to its place while it lives; a '&' may share with other '&'s.

diagnostics.name: LANG_BORROW_NAME_WRITTEN
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is lent out, so its own name may not be written

args.name: name
args.description: the name that was lent out

spec.requirement: A '&mut' is the only reference to its place while it lives; a '&' may share with other '&'s.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LIFETIME_NOT_DETERMINED

spec.requirement: A lifetime in a return type stands in at least one parameter's type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_GENERIC_IS_NOT_A_VALUE

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Generic Functions
spec.requirement: A generic function is not a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_REF_OUTLIVES_PLACE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' outlives '{place}', so it may not be given something that reaches it

args.name: name
args.description: the name being given the reference

args.name: place
args.description: the name whose place the reference names

diagnostics.cause: A reference is only worth having while what it names is still there.  A name bound further out lasts longer than a place made further in, so the place would be gone -- out of reach and no longer nameable -- while the name reaching it is still in hand, and reading through it would reach a variable the program can no longer name.  It is asked of everything that can reach a place: a reference, a tuple holding one, and a lambda, which reaches what it brought in by reference.  It is the rule a function answering with a reference follows, at the third place a reference can escape to.

spec.requirement: A name may hold a reference only to a place that lasts as long as the name.

diagnostics.name: LANG_REF_WRITTEN_INTO_A_PLACE_FROM_OUTSIDE
diagnostics.message: what goes into a place this call did not make may not be a reference of this call's own
diagnostics.cause: The place written here came in from outside, so how long it lasts is the caller's business and nothing in the signature says it.  A reference put there could name something of this call, which the caller would still hold after the call was over -- and neither end can see the mistake: the body cannot see how long the place lasts and the caller cannot see what the body did with it.  What may be written there is a reference that lasts as long as the program, which outlives any caller.

spec.requirement: A reference written into a place the call did not make lasts as long as the program.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYSCALL_BAD_ARGUMENT
diagnostics.message: a request to the kernel is given machine words, and argument {position} is '{found}'

args.name: position
args.description: which argument it is, counting the number as the first

args.name: found
args.description: the type that was written there

diagnostics.cause: What the kernel takes is registers: a number, a descriptor, a length, or the address of something.  Nothing else fits in one, and a floating-point value or a value of a type the program made up would be a program that meant something the kernel cannot be asked.  A reference counts, being an address, and so does a whole number of any width.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYSCALL_TOO_MANY
diagnostics.message: the kernel takes at most {expected} arguments after the number, and this gives {found}
diagnostics.cause: A system call is made by putting its arguments in registers the kernel names, and there are six of them on every architecture this compiler generates for.  A call wanting more is not a call any of them has.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYSCALL_UNKNOWN_NAME
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not a system call this compiler knows a number for

args.name: name
args.description: the name that was asked for

diagnostics.cause: The compiler holds the number each system call has on each architecture, because it is the compiler that knows which architecture it is building for.  What is in that table is what the runtime and the standard library ask for, each number checked against the kernel's own; a call nothing has asked for yet is not there, and adding one is a line per architecture rather than anything a program can do.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYSCALL_NOT_ON_THIS_ARCHITECTURE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is not a system call '{architecture}' has

args.name: name
args.description: the call that was asked for

diagnostics.cause: The call exists on some architecture this compiler generates for and not on this one.  A module that wants it on the ones that have it asks inside an arm the compiler settles, so that the arm is never lowered where the call is not there.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PRODUCT_NO_SUCH_FIELD
diagnostics.message: '{type}' has no field called '{name}'

args.name: name
args.description: the field that was asked for

diagnostics.cause: A record is its fields and nothing else, and which fields it has is what its definition says.  A name that is not one of them names nothing: there is no value to read and nothing to give, whichever end asked.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PRODUCT_FIELD_MISSING
diagnostics.message: '{type}' is made with every field, and '{name}' is not given

args.name: name
args.description: the field nothing was given for

diagnostics.cause: A record is its fields, so a value of one is a value for each of them.  There is no default to fall back on and nothing that would be right to leave behind: a field left out would be storage holding whatever was there, which is the thing this language does not have.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PRODUCT_FIELD_TWICE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is given twice

args.name: name
args.description: the field named more than once

diagnostics.cause: One field, one value.  Two would be a value whose meaning depended on which of them the compiler chose, and there is no reading of it that is not a guess about what was meant.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PRODUCT_FIELD_NOT_NAMED
diagnostics.message: a value of '{type}' names every field it gives
diagnostics.cause: A record's fields have names and its value uses them, so that a value reads as what it is rather than as a list whose order has to be checked against the definition.  A tuple is the shape for several values that go by position.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ORDERED_NOT_A_REFERENCE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' reads or writes through a reference, and this is '{found}'

args.name: name
args.description: which of the two was written

args.name: found
args.description: the type that was written instead

diagnostics.cause: An ordering is said about one access to one place, so what it is given is the place: a reference and nothing else.  A value has no place to order an access to, and a place named outright would be a second way of saying what a reference already says.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ORDERED_NOT_MUTABLE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' writes, and '&mut' is what says a place may be written

args.name: name
args.description: which of the two was written

diagnostics.cause: Writing through a reference that does not allow it is refused wherever it is written, and a releasing write is a write.  The ordering says what other observers see and changes nothing about who may write.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ORDERED_SEVERAL_VALUES
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is one access, and a '{found}' is several values

args.name: name
args.description: which of the two was written

args.name: found
args.description: the type the reference points at

diagnostics.cause: A record, a tuple and a result each travel as the several values they are made of, so reading or writing one is that many accesses.  Which of them the ordering belonged to would have no answer, and ordering all of them is a different promise from the one the word makes.  Order one field, or one index, and let the rest be ordinary.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ADDRESS_NOT_A_TYPE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is told what is there by a lifted type, and this is not one

args.name: name
args.description: which of the two was written

diagnostics.cause: What is at an address is not something the compiler can work out, so the program says it, between the lifting brackets.  A name that turns out to be a variable rather than a type is read as the variable, which is what the brackets are there to make unambiguous.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ADDRESS_NOT_AN_ADDRESS
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is given an address, and this is '{found}'

args.name: name
args.description: which of the two was written

args.name: found
args.description: the type that was written instead

diagnostics.cause: An address is a machine word or a reference: a whole number as wide as one, which is what a request to the kernel answers with, or a place already reached some other way.  A narrower number is not an address, since half of one is not a place.

diagnostics.name: LANG_AT_NOT_A_REFERENCE
diagnostics.message: '⎕at' answers a reference, and '{found}' is not one
diagnostics.cause: The lifted type is what the answer is, so that the type written on the definition and the type written between the brackets are the same words.  What is at an address is one value, reached through a reference; several of them are what '⎕span' answers.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SPAN_NOT_AN_ARRAY
diagnostics.message: '⎕span' answers an array whose length is not in its type, and '{found}' is not one
diagnostics.cause: How many there are is given as an argument, so it cannot also be in the type: an array type that says its length says something the count would then have to agree with, and two statements of one thing can disagree.  One value at an address is what '⎕at' answers.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SPAN_NOT_A_COUNT
diagnostics.message: '⎕span' is given how many there are, and this is '{found}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type that was written instead

diagnostics.cause: How many is a whole number, as every length in this language is.  A negative count has no meaning and a floating-point one has no meaning either.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ASSIGN_NOT_A_RECORD
diagnostics.message: this is not a record that is somewhere, so a field of it has no place to be written
diagnostics.cause: Writing a field writes one place, so what holds the field has to be somewhere: a name given storage of its own, what a reference names, or a field of one of those.  A record the program worked out is a value in registers and has no place for a field to be at; bind it to a name first, which is what gives it one.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WIDEN_NOT_A_TYPE
diagnostics.message: the type '⎕widen' makes a value of is written between '⌜' and '⌝'
diagnostics.cause: What a value is to become is a type and not an expression, and a type's name and a variable's name are both identifiers, so the brackets are what says which was meant.  Without them the meaning of the call would depend on what the names turned out to be.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WIDEN_NOT_AN_INTEGER
diagnostics.message: '⎕widen' makes a whole number out of a whole number, and '{found}' is not one
diagnostics.cause: Widening is about how much room a number has, which is a question only a whole number has an answer to.  A floating-point value of another format is a different question with a different answer, and a value of a type the program made up is not a number at all.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WIDEN_DOES_NOT_FIT
diagnostics.message: not every '{found}' is a '{wanted}', so this is a narrowing and can fail

args.name: wanted
args.description: the type it was to become

diagnostics.cause: '⎕widen' answers the value itself and not a result, which it may do only because it cannot fail: every value of the type written has to be a value of the type wanted.  A narrower type into a wider one of the same signedness is such a case, and so is an unsigned type into a signed one with room to spare.  Anything else -- fewer bits, or a negative number where the type has none -- is a narrowing, and '⎕narrow' is what answers a result saying whether it fitted.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ADDRESS_OF_NOT_A_REFERENCE
diagnostics.message: '⎕address' is given a place, and this is '{found}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type that was written instead

diagnostics.cause: A place is what has an address, and a reference is how this language names one.  A value the program worked out is in a register and has no address to answer with; taking a reference of the name it is bound to is what gives it one.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_NO_BODY
diagnostics.message: '{name}' has no body, so something has to say where it is defined
diagnostics.cause: A function with no body is the declaration of one defined somewhere else, and the only somewhere else this compiler has is the runtime it carries: the 'external' attribute, given a symbol, is what names it.  A function that was meant to have a body is one whose body was left off, and the two read alike until the attribute says which was meant.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_EXTERNAL_HAS_A_BODY
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is defined somewhere else, so it may not be defined here as well
diagnostics.cause: The 'external' attribute says the body lives elsewhere and the compiler fills it in.  A body written here would be a second definition of one thing, and nothing could say which of the two a call reached.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_EXTERNAL_UNKNOWN
diagnostics.message: nothing the compiler carries is called '{symbol}'
diagnostics.cause: What the 'external' attribute may name is what the runtime packaged with the compiler defines; there is no linker and nothing else to reach.  A name that is not one of those is a call to something that will not be there, which is worth saying where it is written rather than leaving to whatever reads the image.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition

diagnostics.name: LANG_ABI_TYPE_BY_VALUE
diagnostics.message: '{type}' is laid out for something else to read, so only a reference to one crosses a call
diagnostics.cause: A record marked with the 'abi' attribute is shared with code compiled by something else, which passes a record by rules of its own -- rules this compiler does not follow and does not have to, since a reference is passed the same way by every one of them.  Bind it to a name and hand over a reference to that name.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types

diagnostics.name: LANG_BYTES_NOT_TEXT
diagnostics.message: '⎕bytes' answers the bytes of text, and this is '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: What a string is made of is bytes, and what it is encoded as is UTF-8, so the bytes of one are a thing to ask for.  Nothing else in this language has bytes to answer with: an array already is its elements, and a number is a number whatever width it is held in.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_BAD_SIZE
diagnostics.message: '{option}' wants a size, and '{given}' is not one
diagnostics.cause: A size is a number of bytes, and may be written with 'K', 'M' or 'G' after it for a multiple of 1024.  It has to be a number: an option given something else is an option whose value came from somewhere that did not know what it was for.

diagnostics.name: LANG_DOC_UNKNOWN_COMMAND
diagnostics.message: '{command}' is not a documentation command

args.name: command
args.description: the word that was written after the sigil

diagnostics.cause: A documentation comment may say what a definition is for in prose and say particular things about it with the commands Doxygen uses -- `\brief`, `\param`, `\return` and a few more, with `\` or `@` in front.  A word that is not one of them is either a mistake or prose that begins with a sigil; what it is not is something a reader of the comment will act on, so it is reported rather than shown as though it meant something.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Documentation comments

diagnostics.name: LANG_DOC_PARAM_UNKNOWN
diagnostics.message: '{command} {name}' names nothing that '{owner}' takes

args.name: command
args.description: the command as it was written

args.name: owner
args.description: the definition the comment belongs to

diagnostics.cause: The comment documents a parameter the function does not have, which is what is left when a parameter is renamed or removed and the comment is not.  Whoever reads it is told about something that is not there.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Documentation comments

diagnostics.name: LANG_DOC_PARAM_TWICE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is documented twice
diagnostics.cause: Two `\param` commands name one parameter, so one of them is about something else -- a parameter that was renamed, or a line copied and not finished.  A reader is shown both and has no way to tell which was meant.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Documentation comments

diagnostics.name: LANG_DOC_RETURN_OF_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: '{command}' on '{owner}', which answers with nothing

args.name: command
args.description: the command as it was written

diagnostics.cause: The comment says what the function answers with and the function answers with nothing: it has no arrow, which is how a function says so.  Either the arrow was meant to be there or the line was.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Documentation comments

diagnostics.name: LANG_DOC_NOT_A_FUNCTION
diagnostics.message: '{command}' on '{owner}', which is not a function

args.name: command
args.description: the command as it was written

args.name: owner
args.description: the definition the comment belongs to

diagnostics.cause: Parameters and what is answered with are things a function has; a type, a variable or a unit has neither, so a comment on one that speaks of them was written for something else or was left behind when the definition changed.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Documentation comments

diagnostics.name: LANG_STMT_UNREACHABLE
diagnostics.message: statements after this one are never executed
diagnostics.cause: The statement before this one leaves the block it stands in -- 'return' leaves the function, 'break' leaves a loop, 'continue' begins the loop's next turn -- so nothing after it in that block can run.  This is usually leftover code, or a jump that was meant to be conditional.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_REDUNDANT
diagnostics.message: 'return' can and should be omitted on the last statement of a function
diagnostics.cause: When the value of the last statement is the function's result, the 'return' keyword carries no information and is omitted in the canonical form of the language.  The compiler's own output never writes it.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_MISSING
diagnostics.message: control reaches the end of '{name}' without producing a value of type '{type}'
diagnostics.cause: A function whose return type is not 'void' must produce a value on every path that leaves it.  Because the language admits no undefined behaviour, falling off the end is an error rather than an unspecified result.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_VALUE_IN_VOID
diagnostics.message: returning a value from '{name}', which is declared to return 'void'
diagnostics.cause: The function declares no result, so there is nothing for the returned value to become.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_STMT_VALUE_DISCARDED
diagnostics.message: the value of this statement is not used
diagnostics.cause: An expression computes a value and does nothing else, so a statement that is nothing but an expression is a statement with no effect unless something takes the value.  Something does take it in exactly one place: the last statement of a body is the body's result.  Everywhere else the value goes nowhere, and a line that goes nowhere is either a mistake or a leftover -- a generator that emits one has a defect, which is the reason this is an error rather than a warning.  Where the line is meant to stand as it is, `@[ignore(5005)]` on the statement says so.

spec.section: The Language / Expressions / Statements that are expressions
spec.requirement: A statement that is an expression must have its value used; the last statement of a body is the body's result.

diagnostics.name: LANG_STMT_ASSIGNMENT_IS_AN_ARROW
diagnostics.message: '=' compares two values; an assignment is written '←'
diagnostics.cause: Attached where the discarded value is a comparison written with '=', which is what someone writes who has spent years in a language where '=' assigns.  The diagnostic itself says the value goes nowhere; this says why the line was probably written.

spec.requirement: An assignment is written `NAME ← VALUE`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED
diagnostics.message: the bootstrap compiler cannot generate code for {construct} yet

args.name: construct
args.description: the construct that has no code generation yet

diagnostics.cause: The bootstrap compiler implements only as much of the language as the compiler's own source needs, so a construct the specification describes may still have no code generation.  This is a limitation of the bootstrap compiler and not an error in the program; the same program will compile once the construct is implemented.

spec.requirement: It does not have to be able to handle the entire language as per the specification as long as it can compile the code of the actual compiler.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_BACKEND_NEEDS_AN_EXTENSION
diagnostics.message: this needs the {extension} extension, and the program is built for '{level}', which has not got it

args.name: extension
args.description: what the code generator would have needed

args.name: level
args.description: what the program was asked to be built for

diagnostics.cause: On an architecture whose base is small and whose every capability is an extension, what a program may use is what it was built for.  Where it uses something the extensions do not cover, the answer is not to emit it anyway -- that is a program that does not run -- and not to emulate it either, since an emulation of a floating-point convention is a different calling convention and a different ABI.  So it is refused, and the two ways out are to build for something that has the extension, with '--mclevel', or to write the program without whatever wanted it.

spec.requirement: A program uses only what the ISA it is built for provides.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_BACKEND_UNENCODABLE
diagnostics.message: instruction cannot be encoded: {detail}
diagnostics.cause: The instruction, its operands, or the combination of the two cannot be represented in the target's encoding.  From generated code this reports a defect in the compiler; once inline assembly exists it will also report a constraint the written instruction violates, such as naming a high-byte register in a form that carries a REX prefix.

spec.requirement: The backends should use a symbolic version to generate the assembler code to allow, in future, inline assembler code.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_IMAGE_UNDEFINED_SYMBOL
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is referenced but never defined
diagnostics.cause: Compilation covers the whole program at once and there is no equivalent of an object file, so every symbol the generated code refers to must be defined by the same compilation.  A symbol that is still undefined at image generation means a function the program calls was never given a body.

spec.requirement: At least for the time being there is only whole-program compilation.  There is no equivalent of object files.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_IMAGE_VALUE_OUT_OF_RANGE
diagnostics.message: a value of {value} does not fit the {field} field that must hold it

args.name: value
args.description: the value that does not fit

diagnostics.cause: A displacement, an address or an initial value has to fit the field the instruction or the image reserves for it.  One that does not is reported rather than stored with its upper bits dropped: a program that branched to an address other than the one it named, or started with a value other than the one it was given, would be behaving otherwise than it reads.  A branch too far to reach is the usual cause, and needs a longer form of the instruction, which this compiler does not choose yet.  That a value fits where it is stored is one of the checks the compiler always performs, rather than one it leaves to the reader to have made.

spec.requirement: The compiler predominently has to be fast while at the same time always perform all conformance checks and generating small code.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_INTERNAL_ERROR
diagnostics.message: internal compiler error: {detail}
diagnostics.cause: The compiler detected an inconsistency in its own data structures, which always indicates a defect in the compiler rather than in the compiled program.  Please report it together with the source that triggered it.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_UNIMPLEMENTED_FEATURE
diagnostics.message: {feature} is not implemented yet

args.name: feature
args.description: the feature the specification describes but the compiler lacks

diagnostics.cause: The specification describes this, and the compiler does not implement it yet.  It reports a gap in the compiler rather than a defect in the program: the same program will compile once the feature exists.

spec.requirement: It does not have to be able to handle the entire language as per the specification as long as it can compile the code of the actual compiler.
